content.text: Dr Khan also quoted World Health Organization (WHO) message for the World TB day"Lets Unite to Stop TB" and further mentioned that this year the focus is on joint work with all partners in TB control by requesting everybody to unite to use DOTS. Elaborating on the effects of drug resistant strains of TB, Dr Khan said that it is caused by inconsistent or partial treatment patients do not take their medicines regularly for the required period because the. Start to feel better. Doctors prescribe wrong drugs or the wrong combination of drugs or the drug supply is unreliable. Dr Khan revealed that "a drug resistant TB is very difficult to control and more expensive to treat, and is more likely to be fatal in a country like Pakistan". He added that from a public health point of view "poorly supervised, incomplete treatment of TB is worse than no treatment at all"

A study done at AKUH showed that one-third strains of Mycobacterium TB were found to be resistant to at least one anti-TB drug. Dr Khan recommended that directly observed treatment Short course (DOTS), where a health care worker observes patient taking their medicines is the best method for preventing drug resistance.

Dr Naseerudin Mahmood, Consultant Child Specialist at AKUH also confirmed that drug resistance is also a serious problem in children. He highlighted the importance of chemoprophylaxis in preventing spread of TB in children. Dr Mahmood informed that most of the children get this disease from their parents or some adult family member or contact. He advised that BCG vaccine should be administered to every child soon after birth to prevent TB meningitis and miliary TB. He further stressed that every effort should be made to identify the index case.

Dr Majeed Memon, Consultant Chest Physician, raised concern over rising TB in women. He informed that TB kills more women than all causes of maternal mortality combined. Dr Memon added that unfortunately in our country, stigma attached to TB leads to isolation, abandonment and divorce of women. He urged the media to spread the knowledge about TB among general public.
Dr Arif Sarwari, Consultant Infectious Diseases, highlighted the importance of sputum microscopy in making the diagnosis of pulmonary TB.

content.title: Tuberculosis epidemic threatens Pakistan
content.author: Ambreen Nadeem
content.description: "Drug resistant strains of Tuberculosis (TB) is sweeping through Pakistan and unless some urgent action is taken, it could pose a major threat to the entire population of Pakistan", revealed Dr Javaid Ahmed Khan, Associate Professor and Consultant Chest Physician of the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH) He was giving a presentation on "Tuberculosis Epidemic Threatens Pakistan" at "Signs, Symptoms and Care", a monthly public health awareness program, held on March 19, 1999 at the Aga Khan University Hospital. Dr Khan informed that "there are at least two million cases of active TB in Pakistan and every year 350.000 patients are added to this pool".
